subject: Culture
title: Valentine's Day Commerce
description: Learn Valentine's Day Commerce in one minute.

hook.text: Japan's Valentine's Day requires women to give men chocolate. Men return the favor on March 14—White Day.

buildup.text: Valentine's Day was a minor saint's feast until Hallmark began selling cards in the early 1900s.

discovery.text: The modern holiday was manufactured by greeting card, chocolate, and flower industries working in coordination.

twist.text: South Korea added Black Day on April 14. Singles who received nothing eat black noodles together in solidarity.

climax.text: Valentine's spending hit $26 billion in the US in 2023. Love became the most profitable emotion to commercialize.

punchline.text: Romance is the best-selling product ever packaged.

quiz.question: What is celebrated on March 14 in Japan?

details.summary: Valentine's Day generates over $25 billion in annual US spending — a commercial juggernaut built from a medieval saint's feast day. Greeting card companies, chocolate manufacturers, and florists have transformed romantic obligation into an economic engine.
details.whyItMatters: Valentine's Day exemplifies how commercial interests capture cultural traditions and create new consumption obligations. Its global variations reveal how the same holiday adapts to different gender norms.
takeaways: Valentine's Day generates over $25 billion in US spending annually
Hallmark did not create Valentine's Day but industrialized it
In Japan, women give chocolate to men, with men reciprocating on White Day

faq.question: How did Valentine's Day become commercialized?
faq.answer: Valentine's cards existed since the 18th century, but mass production in the 1840s by Esther Howland created an industry. Cadbury introduced heart-shaped chocolate boxes. Florists promoted red roses.

faq.question: How does Valentine's Day work in Japan?
faq.answer: Japanese Valentine's Day (introduced by chocolate companies in the 1950s) requires women to give chocolate to men — both romantic (honmei-choco) and obligatory workplace gifts (giri-choco). Men reciprocate on White Day (March 14) with gifts expected to be two to three times more valuable.
